q: What is the usual warranty length of the compressor in a split-type air conditioner?
n: Per the exam key, split-type air conditioner compressors usually carry a 10-year warranty. Exact terms vary by manufacturer and model. Source: Philippine air-conditioner manufacturers' published warranty terms (e.g., Carrier, Koppel, LG).

q: What is the usual warranty length of the compressor of a window type air conditioner?
n: Per the exam key, window-type compressors usually carry a 5-year warranty, shorter than split-type units. Exact terms vary by manufacturer. Source: Philippine air-conditioner manufacturers' published warranty terms.

q: What is the purpose of a light curtain sensor in an industrial setting?
n: A light curtain sensor, also known as a safety light barrier or light grid, is commonly used in industrial settings to detect motion and ensure the safety of workers and equipment. When an object breaks the light beam of the sensor, it sends a signal to the machine to stop or slow down, preventing accidents and injuries. A light curtain is an array of infrared beams. It senses when a person or object enters a hazardous zone (presence or motion detection) and stops the machine. Source: IEC 61496 (Safety of Machinery – Electro-sensitive Protective Equipment).

q: How long is the included copper tube when purchasing a split-type air conditioner without any additional charges?
n: Per the exam key, a standard split-type installation package includes about 3.0 m of copper refrigerant tubing. Longer runs are charged per meter. Source: Philippine dealers' standard installation packages; ASHRAE Handbook – HVAC Systems and Equipment (Ductless Split Systems).

q: Which of the following links the elevator car and the controller for power and signal transmission?
n: The traveling cable is the flexible cable that hangs from the elevator car to the hoistway. It carries power and signals between the car and the controller. Source: ASME A17.1 (Safety Code for Elevators); PEC Part 1, Art. 6.20 (Elevators).

q: Which wood joint is most commonly used for trim and molding parts?
n: Since the miter joint has minimal strength, it is typically used for trim and molding purposes. Depending on the purpose, you may need to strengthen the miter joint by adding nails. A classic example of mitered butt joinery is the wooden picture frames. Miter joints meet at 45° so the profile runs continuously around a corner with no end grain showing. That makes them the standard joint for trim and moldings, though they are weak without fasteners. Source: Spence, Carpentry and Building Construction (Joinery); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 10.

q: Which wood joint is similar to toe-nailing?
n: Pocket joint (aka pocket hole joint or pocket screw joint) is basically similar to toe nailing but using screws. Consequently, the uses of pocket hole joinery in the construction of a project are almost unlimited. Assembling structural frames and cabinet face frames is a common application. A pocket (pocket-hole) joint drives a screw at a steep angle from one member into the other. It is the screwed version of toe-nailing. Source: Fine Woodworking joinery references; Spence, Carpentry and Building Construction.

q: Which of the following is the most common application of biscuit joint?
n: Biscuit joints set an oval compressed-wood biscuit, glued, into matching slots. They are most used to align and join boards edge to edge, as in panels and tabletops. Source: Fine Woodworking joinery references; Hoadley, Understanding Wood.

q: Which joint is usually pre-made and ready to use, cut with a table saw, and commonly used for flooring?
n: Tongue-and-groove flooring comes from the mill already machined, with tongues and grooves cut on a shaper or table saw. It is laid ready-to-install. Source: NWFA Installation Guidelines; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 10 (Wood Flooring).

q: Which of the following is the least strong wood joint?
n: The three strongest wood joints are dovetail joint, box joint and mortise and tenon joint. Of the choices, the plain lap joint is the weakest. Dovetail, box (finger) and mortise-and-tenon joints interlock and have far more glue area. Source: Spence, Carpentry and Building Construction (Joinery strength); Hoadley, Understanding Wood.

q: Which of the following is the maker of liquid tile?
n: Per the exam key, Liquid Tile is a Davies Paints product. Source: Davies Paints Philippines product catalog.

q: Liquid tile is what type of coating?
n: Per the exam key, Liquid Tile is a solvent-based acrylic coating. Solvent-based acrylics give a hard, tile-like gloss and resist water and stains. Source: Davies Paints Philippines product data sheet; PDCA Painting Standards (Coating Types).

q: What is the usual minimum thickness of gypsum boards commercially available?
n: Per the exam key, 9 mm is the thinnest gypsum board commonly stocked locally for ceilings. 12 mm is standard for walls and fire-rated work. Source: Philippine gypsum board manufacturers' catalogs (e.g., USG Boral, Gyproc); ASTM C1396 (Gypsum Board).

q: It refers to the framework of the cabinet, onto which doors are hung and drawers are fitted.
n: The carcass is the box frame of a cabinet (sides, top, bottom and back) on which doors are hung and drawers fitted. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Carcass); Architectural Woodwork Standards (AWI).

q: Which is the most ideal paint for textured paint finish?
n: Textured finishes are commonly applied with solvent-based acrylic coatings. They build thickness, hold the pattern and weather well outdoors. Source: MPI Architectural Painting Specification Manual (Textured Coatings); manufacturers' technical data.

q: In construction, it refers to the set of planned and systematic activities laid out before the building project starts. It aims to assure that the quality requirements of the building will be fulfilled.
n: Although you might be more familiar with QA/QC Engineers on site, Quality Assurance and Quality Control are two different but related things. Both are part of any product quality management program that ensures that the finished products (buildings in case of construction industry) comply with several quality standards. In comparison to quality assurance defined above, quality control entails observation techniques and activities which aim to identify whether the final product actually fulfills customer requirements. Quality control also identifies the need for corrective measures. In other words, quality control monitors work as it happens and ensures that the results satisfy the requirements specified. Quality assurance is the set of planned, systematic activities set up before work starts to make sure quality requirements will be met. Quality control is the inspection and testing of the actual work. Source: ISO 9000 (Quality Management – Vocabulary); DPWH Quality Assurance Unit guidelines.

q: What can be added to concrete to make it lightweight?
n: Perlite is an example of a lightweight aggregate. Using this makes the concrete product lighter. Other examples of light aggregates are expanded shale, slate, vermiculite etc.). Perlite is an expanded volcanic-glass aggregate. Replacing normal aggregate with it produces lightweight, insulating concrete. Source: ACI 213R (Structural Lightweight Aggregate Concrete); Kosmatka et al., Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (PCA).

q: Which is the most reliable tool for compacting concrete?
n: Compaction or consolidation is the process which expels entrapped air from freshly placed concrete and packs the aggregate particles together so as to increase the density of concrete. It significantly increases the ultimate strength of concrete and enhances the bond with reinforcement. Among the choices, needle vibrator is the only concrete compaction tool. Take note that plate compactor is used for soil compaction, not for concrete. An internal (needle or poker) vibrator is the standard, most reliable tool for consolidating fresh concrete. It removes entrapped air and packs the mix around the bars. Plate compactors are for soil. Source: ACI 309R (Guide for Consolidation of Concrete).

q: The water-cement ratio is inversely proportional to
n: The best answer here is strength. As the W/C ratio increases, the strength decreases. Therefore, both are inversely proportional. Increasing the water- cement ratio also increases consistency and workability, but no effect on hydration,. Strength falls as the water-cement ratio rises (Abrams' law), so the two are inversely related. Workability rises with more water. Source: Kosmatka et al., Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (PCA), Ch. 9; Abrams (1918).

q: An RC column has a height of 3.3 m. Lapping of the main vertical bars should be located
o: At 2.0m up to 2.7m level of column
At 0.825m up to 1.65m level of column
At 1.1m up to 2.2m level of column
At 0.825m up to 2.475m level of column
n: Lapping of rebars should happen within the lapping zone of an RC column. Lapping zone starts from L/4 distance from the bottom of the column and L/4 distance from the top of the column. L is the height of the column. L/4 = 3.3 / 4 = 0.825m. Therefore, the correct answer is at 0.825m up to 2.475m level of column. Column bar splices are placed in the middle half of the clear height, away from the high-moment ends. For L = 3.3 m: L/4 = 0.825 m, so laps go from 0.825 m to 2.475 m. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 418.7.4.3 (Special moment frame column lap splices – middle half); ACI 318.

q: Which among these woods is most commonly used as a door jamb?
n: Tanguile (red lauan) is moderately hard, stable and economical. It is the commonly used wood for door jambs, casings and frames. Source: DENR-FPRDI, Philippine Woods (Tanguile uses); Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (Lumber).

q: It is an imported wood similar in texture and color as Narra.
n: Rosewood (Dalbergia) is an imported hardwood whose reddish-brown color and fine texture resemble narra, so it is often compared to it. Source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, Ch. 2 (Rosewood); DENR-FPRDI, Philippine Woods.

q: This is also known as Philippine Ebony. Known for its dark color, strength and impact resistance, it is now endangered and very expensive.
n: Kamagong (Diospyros blancoi) is the Philippine ebony. The dark wood is dense, hard and impact-resistant, and it is now scarce and costly. Source: DENR-FPRDI, Philippine Woods; DENR Administrative Order on threatened species.

q: Lauan, a common Philippine hardwood, is usually available in two variations.
n: Lauan is traded as red lauan (such as tanguile) and white lauan (such as almon and mayapis). Source: DENR-FPRDI, Philippine Woods (Philippine Mahogany group).

q: How can the grain of Narra be described?
n: Narra (Pterocarpus indicus) has an interlocked, wavy grain that gives its prized figure. Source: DENR-FPRDI, Philippine Woods (Narra); USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook.

q: Which of the following materials is the least brittle?
n: Steel is not brittle but ductile. Brittleness describes the property of a material that fractures when subjected to stress but has a little tendency to deform before rupture. Steel is ductile: it deforms considerably before it breaks. Glass, ceramic and granite are brittle and fracture with little deformation. Source: Callister, Materials Science and Engineering; Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction.

q: Cellulose insulation is most commonly installed or used in what form?
n: It is usually called loose fill cellulose insulation. Cellulose insulation is most often installed as loose fill, blown into attics and dense-packed into wall cavities. Source: ASTM C739 (Cellulosic Fiber Loose-Fill Thermal Insulation); US DOE, Insulation Types.

q: Which type of thermal insulation is naturally fire resistant?
n: Although loose fill insulation can be made of fiberglass, other materials are also available such as cellulose which is not naturally fire resistant. Fiberglass is made of glass fibers and is inherently noncombustible. Cellulose needs fire-retardant treatment, and spray foams are combustible. Source: US DOE, Insulation Materials; ASTM E136 (Noncombustibility).

q: Which type of thermal insulation contains about 80% recycled material?
n: Cellulose insulation often claims to have 80% or more recycled material. Another type of insulation with high recycled material content is rockwool which is 70- 90%. Fiberglass has 40-60% recycled content while spray foam usually has very little. Cellulose insulation is made mostly of recycled newsprint and paper, typically 80% or more recycled content. Source: US DOE, Insulation Materials (Cellulose); Cellulose Insulation Manufacturers Association.

q: Which of the following must be professionally installed?
n: Among the choices, spray foam is the most complicated to install therefore it must be professionally installed. Spray foam must be installed by trained professionals. The chemical components react on site and need proper ratios, temperature, ventilation and protective equipment. Source: US DOE, Insulation Materials (Spray Foam); Spray Polyurethane Foam Alliance installation guidelines.

q: What is the most economical heavy equipment that can be used for demolition of an existing single storey RC structure?
n: While an excavator is usually used for excavating, its bucket attachment can be replaced with a breaker to help in demolition. An excavator, fitted with a bucket, breaker or crusher, is the most economical single machine for demolishing a small one-storey RC structure and loading the debris. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods (Demolition Equipment).

q: A soil stabilization method using in situ soilcrete columns.
n: Jet grouting creates in situ columns of soilcrete (grouted soil), using a grouting monitor attached to the end of a drill stem (basically injecting the soil). Jet grouting injects grout at very high pressure through a rotating monitor. It mixes with the soil to form in-situ soilcrete columns. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering (Ground Improvement – Jet Grouting).

q: What is the natural state of soil for building construction?
n: Natural means undisturbed. Undisturbed soil is generally moist. Undisturbed natural ground is usually moist, holding its natural moisture content. That is the reference state used in excavation and earthwork estimates. Source: Das, Principles of Geotechnical Engineering (natural moisture content); Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (Earthworks).

q: Who accredits testing laboratories for construction materials?
n: Particularly the BRS or Bureau of Research and Standards under the DPWH. The DPWH Bureau of Research and Standards accredits construction-materials testing laboratories for public works. Source: DPWH Department Orders on accreditation of testing laboratories (Bureau of Research and Standards).

q: A structure holding back earth to prevent it from sliding or eroding away.
n: A retaining wall holds back soil or rock on one side to keep it from sliding or eroding where the ground changes level. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering (Retaining Walls); Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which refers to a portion of a flat surface recessed or sunk below the surrounding area, distinctly set off by molding or some other decorative device?
n: All these definitions of “panel” are from the Dictionary of Architecture and Construction, a book by Cyirll Harris. One meaning of "panel" is a section of a flat surface recessed below, or raised above, the surrounding area and set off by molding or another decorative edge. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Panel).

q: Which term refers to a large, relatively thin board or sheet of lumber, plywood or other material used as a wall covering?
n: All these definitions of “panel” are from the Dictionary of Architecture and Construction, a book by Cyirll Harris. "Panel" also means a large, relatively thin board or sheet of lumber, plywood or other material used as a wall covering. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Panel).

q: Which term refers to a section of a floor, wall, ceiling or roof, usually prefabricated and of large size, handled as a single unit in the operations of assembly and erection?
n: All these definitions of “panel” are from the Dictionary of Architecture and Construction, a book by Cyirll Harris. "Panel" also refers to a large, usually prefabricated section of floor, wall, ceiling or roof handled as one unit during assembly and erection. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Panel).

q: What do you call a wedge-shaped step in stair construction?
n: A winder is a wedge-shaped tread used to turn a stair without a landing. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (Stair); NBCP Rule XII / RA 9514 RIRR (winders in exits).

q: A decorative bottom step in a stair construction.
n: A curtail step is the bottom step of a stair with a scroll-shaped end that projects beyond the newel. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Curtail Step); Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: A safety device of an escalator located between the landing platform and the moving escalator steps.
n: The comb plate is at each landing where the steps enter. Its teeth mesh with the cleated steps so objects and fingers cannot be drawn into the gap. Source: ASME A17.1 (Escalators – Comb Plates); EN 115-1.

q: What is the standard maximum spacing of screws in drywall installation?
n: The general rule of thumb is that screws in a drywall installation are usually spaced in 300mm to 400mm (12” to 16”) distance. Drywall screws are spaced at most about 300 mm (12 in) on ceilings and 400 mm (16 in) on walls. 400 mm is the standard maximum. Source: GA-216 (Gypsum Association – Application of Gypsum Panel Products); ASTM C840.

q: In construction, what is a document that seeks the clarification of plans, drawings, specifications, and agreements?
n: RFI means Request for Information. A Request for Information (RFI) is the formal document a contractor uses to ask for clarification of drawings, specifications or contract terms. Source: AIA Document G716 (Request for Information); construction administration practice.

q: Which of the following is true about elevator installation?
o: In most cases, the steel framework for the elevator is usually built first before the elevator shaft walls
A machine room above the shaft is a requirement
The limit switch is used to prevent overspeeding of the elevator car
The governor is activated when the maximum speed of the car is exceeded
n: The overspeed governor trips when the car exceeds its rated speed by a set margin. It then sets the car safeties. Limit switches stop over-travel, not overspeed, and machine-room-less elevators exist. Source: ASME A17.1 (Governors and Car Safeties); Stein & Reynolds, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings.

q: Who can prepare, sign and certify the FSCR, FSCCR and FSMR?
n: Under the Fire Code RIRR, the Fire Safety Compliance Report (FSCR), the Fire Safety Compliance and Commissioning Report (FSCCR) and the Fire Safety Maintenance Report (FSMR) are prepared, signed and certified by a BFP-certified Fire Safety Practitioner. Source: RA 9514 (Fire Code) 2019 RIRR, Rule 9 and Rule 10 (Fire Safety Practitioners).
